unit.name: Core Technical Principles
unit.subtitle: Technology, energy, materials, systems and mechanics

lessons.title: New & Emerging Technologies
lessons.description: How new technologies shape industry, enterprise, society and the environment.
lessons.content_html:
New & Emerging Technologies

Design and technology is constantly evolving. New and emerging technologies change the way products are designed, manufactured and used. As a designer, you need to understand how these developments affect industry, enterprise, society and the environment — and how they influence the choices you make.

Impact on Industry

Automation and robotics have transformed the modern workplace. Factories now use robotic arms for repetitive tasks like welding car bodies or picking items in warehouses. This increases speed, consistency and reduces human error, but it also means fewer manual jobs on production lines.

New technologies have changed the design of buildings and workplaces too. Open-plan offices with digital collaboration tools allow flexible working. Factories are designed around automated systems, with safety zones separating robots from human workers. Tools and equipment have also evolved — 3D printers, laser cutters and CNC routers are now common in both industry and school workshops.

Key Fact

Automation increases production speed, improves consistency and reduces labour costs, but it can lead to job losses in manufacturing.

Enterprise & Innovation

Enterprise means developing a business idea and turning it into a product or service. New technologies have created new ways for designers to fund and sell their work. Crowd funding platforms like Kickstarter allow designers to raise money directly from potential customers before manufacturing begins. This reduces financial risk and tests whether there is a real market for the product.

Virtual marketing and retail allow businesses to reach global audiences through websites and social media without needing a physical shop. Co-operatives and fair trade models use technology to connect producers in developing countries directly with consumers, ensuring fairer pay.

A designer creates a new portable phone charger using solar panels. They set up a Kickstarter campaign with a target of £10,000. Backers pledge money in exchange for early access to the product. If the target is reached, the designer uses the funds to manufacture the charger. If not, no money changes hands. This model removes the need for bank loans or investors.

Sustainability & the Environment

Every product uses resources. Designers must consider whether those resources are finite (like oil and metal ores) or non-finite (like timber and cotton). The disposal of waste is also a major concern — landfill, incineration and ocean pollution all damage the environment.

Sustainable design aims to reduce negative environmental impact. This includes using recycled materials, designing for disassembly so parts can be reused, and minimising packaging. The ecological and social footprint of a product covers everything from raw material extraction to disposal.

Key Fact

Finite resources (oil, metal ores) will run out. Non-finite resources (timber, cotton) can be replenished if managed responsibly. Designers must consider resource type when selecting materials.

Technology Push & Market Pull

Technology push happens when a new invention drives product development — for example, the invention of graphene leading to new ultra-strong, lightweight products. Market pull is the opposite: consumer demand drives innovation, such as the demand for eco-friendly packaging leading to biodegradable alternatives.

Society, Culture & Ethical Design

Products must be designed to avoid negative impacts on people. This means considering the needs of disabled users, elderly people and different religious or cultural groups. Inclusive design ensures products work for as many people as possible.

Designers also face ethical decisions. Planned obsolescence — deliberately designing products to break or become outdated — generates repeat sales but creates waste. Ethical designers consider maintenance, repairability and the full lifecycle of their products.

Modern manufacturing uses several key systems. CAD (computer aided design) allows products to be modelled digitally before making. CAM (computer aided manufacture) uses computers to control machinery like CNC routers and laser cutters. FMS (flexible manufacturing systems) allow production lines to switch between different products quickly. JIT (just in time) manufacturing orders materials only when needed, reducing storage costs. Lean manufacturing aims to eliminate all waste from the production process.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Section A, questions on new and emerging technologies are often worth 1–2 marks and test definitions or quick recall. Make sure you can define terms like automation, CAD, CAM, crowd funding and planned obsolescence. For longer questions, always link the technology to its impact — don’t just describe it, explain why it matters for designers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Automation, robotics, CAD and CAM have transformed how products are designed and manufactured in industry.
  • Enterprise technologies like crowd funding, virtual marketing and fair trade connect designers directly with consumers and producers worldwide.
  • Designers must consider sustainability (finite vs non-finite resources), ethics (planned obsolescence) and inclusive design (disability, culture, religion) in every project.

lessons.title: Energy Generation & Storage
lessons.description: Fossil fuels, nuclear, renewables and energy storage systems for product design.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Generation & Storage

Every product that uses power needs an energy source. As a designer, you must understand how energy is generated and stored so you can select the right power system for your product. This lesson covers fossil fuels, nuclear power, renewable energy and energy storage systems.

Fossil Fuels

Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — are burned in power stations to heat water, producing steam that turns turbines connected to generators. They currently supply a large share of the UK’s electricity. Coal produces the most carbon dioxide per unit of energy, while natural gas is the cleanest of the three.

Key Fact

Arguments for fossil fuels: reliable, high energy output, existing infrastructure. Arguments against: finite resources that will run out, release greenhouse gases causing climate change, extraction damages habitats.

Nuclear Power

Nuclear power generates electricity through nuclear fission — splitting atoms of uranium to release heat, which produces steam to drive turbines. A small amount of fuel generates a huge amount of energy, and nuclear power stations produce no carbon dioxide during operation.

However, nuclear power produces radioactive waste that remains dangerous for thousands of years and must be stored securely. Building and decommissioning nuclear power stations is extremely expensive, and accidents (though rare) can have catastrophic consequences.

Renewable Energy

Renewable energy comes from sources that will not run out. The main types are:

Wind power uses turbines to convert kinetic energy from the wind into electricity. Wind farms can be onshore or offshore. They produce no emissions during operation but depend on weather conditions and can affect wildlife.

Solar power uses photovoltaic cells to convert sunlight into electricity, or solar thermal panels to heat water. Solar panels are silent and low-maintenance but only generate power during daylight and are less effective in cloudy climates.

Tidal power harnesses the movement of tides using barrages or underwater turbines. Tides are predictable, making this a reliable source, but installation costs are high and it can affect marine ecosystems.

Hydroelectric power uses flowing or falling water (usually from a dam) to turn turbines. It is highly reliable and can respond quickly to demand, but large dams flood valleys and displace communities.

Biomass generates energy by burning organic materials such as wood, crops or waste. It is considered carbon neutral because the plants absorbed CO₂ while growing, but it still produces air pollution and requires large areas of land for fuel crops.

Key Fact

The five main renewable energy sources are wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric and biomass. All produce little or no greenhouse gas emissions during operation, but each has limitations related to cost, reliability or environmental impact.

Energy Storage Systems

Energy must often be stored for later use. Kinetic pumped storage systems pump water uphill to a reservoir when electricity demand is low (often at night). When demand rises, the water is released downhill through turbines to generate electricity almost instantly. Dinorwig in Wales is a well-known example.

Alkaline batteries are single-use batteries found in everyday products like torches and remote controls. Rechargeable batteries (such as lithium-ion) can be charged and discharged hundreds of times, making them essential for portable electronics, electric vehicles and power tools.

When selecting an energy source for a product, designers consider: the power requirement (how much energy is needed), portability (does the product move?), environmental impact, cost, availability and reliability. A portable speaker needs a rechargeable battery; a factory needs mains electricity from the grid. The choice of energy source is always a compromise between these factors.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on energy often ask you to compare sources or give arguments for and against. Always structure your answer clearly — state the advantage or disadvantage, then explain why it matters for the designer or the environment. Don’t just list facts; link them to the context of the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) are reliable but finite and produce greenhouse gases; nuclear power is low-carbon but creates radioactive waste.
  • Renewable sources (wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric, biomass) produce little or no emissions but each has limitations around cost, reliability or environmental impact.
  • Energy storage options include kinetic pumped storage, alkaline batteries and rechargeable (lithium-ion) batteries — the choice depends on the product’s power needs, portability and environmental considerations.

lessons.title: Modern & Smart Materials
lessons.description: Graphene, smart materials, composites and technical textiles in modern design.
lessons.content_html:
Modern & Smart Materials

Material science is advancing rapidly. Designers now have access to materials that would have seemed impossible a few decades ago — from ultra-strong, atom-thin sheets of carbon to fabrics that conduct electricity. This lesson covers modern materials, smart materials, composites and technical textiles.

Modern Materials

Modern materials are developed through new inventions or improvements to existing processes. They offer properties that traditional materials cannot match.

Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern. It is around 200 times stronger than steel, extremely lightweight, flexible, and conducts both heat and electricity brilliantly. Potential applications include flexible screens, ultra-fast electronics and stronger composite materials.

Metal foams are metals (usually aluminium) with gas-filled pores throughout their structure. They are lightweight but strong, and absorb energy well — making them useful for crash protection in vehicles and lightweight structural panels.

Titanium is a strong, lightweight metal that resists corrosion. It is widely used in aerospace, medical implants (hip joints, dental implants) and high-performance sports equipment like bicycle frames.

Key Fact

Key modern materials: graphene (ultra-strong, flexible, conductive), metal foams (lightweight, energy-absorbing), titanium (strong, lightweight, corrosion-resistant). All were developed through improved manufacturing processes.

Other modern materials include coated metals (metals with protective surface layers for corrosion resistance), liquid crystal displays (LCDs) and nanomaterials — materials engineered at the atomic scale to achieve enhanced properties like water resistance or self-cleaning surfaces.

Smart Materials

Smart materials react to changes in their environment. Unlike modern materials, which have fixed enhanced properties, smart materials change their behaviour in response to external stimuli.

Shape memory alloys (SMAs) can be bent or deformed but return to their original shape when heated. Nitinol (a nickel-titanium alloy) is the most common example, used in dental braces, spectacle frames and stents.

Thermochromic pigments change colour when the temperature changes. They are used in colour-changing mugs, baby spoons (to warn if food is too hot) and forehead thermometer strips.

Photochromic pigments change colour in response to light. The most common application is reactive sunglasses lenses that darken in bright sunlight and return to clear indoors.

Key Fact

Smart materials respond to external stimuli: shape memory alloys react to heat, thermochromic pigments react to temperature, and photochromic pigments react to light. The key difference from modern materials is that smart materials change reversibly.

Composite Materials

Composite materials combine two or more materials to create something with better properties than either original. Glass reinforced plastic (GRP) combines glass fibres with a polyester resin matrix. It is lightweight, strong and corrosion-resistant — used for boat hulls, car body panels and storage tanks. Carbon fibre reinforced plastic (CRP) uses carbon fibres instead of glass, making it even stronger and lighter (but more expensive). CRP is used in Formula 1 cars, aircraft components and high-end bicycles.

Technical Textiles

Technical textiles are fabrics engineered for performance rather than appearance. Conductive fabrics have metallic fibres woven in and are used in wearable electronics. Fire-resistant fabrics are treated to resist ignition and are used in firefighter clothing. Kevlar is an extremely strong synthetic fibre used in bulletproof vests, cut-resistant gloves and motorcycle protective gear.

Microfibres are ultra-fine synthetic fibres used in sportswear and cleaning cloths. Micro encapsulation embeds tiny capsules of substances (like fragrance, insect repellent or moisturiser) into fabric, releasing them gradually with wear.

A baby feeding spoon uses thermochromic pigment on the bowl of the spoon. When food is above a safe temperature (around 40°C), the spoon changes colour to warn the parent. Once the food cools to a safe temperature, the spoon returns to its original colour. This is a smart material application because the colour change is reversible and triggered by an external stimulus (heat).
lessons.exam_tip_html: The exam often asks you to distinguish between modern, smart and composite materials. Remember: modern materials have enhanced fixed properties (graphene, titanium), smart materials change reversibly in response to stimuli (SMAs, thermochromic), and composites combine two materials for improved performance (GRP, CRP). Always give a specific example and its application.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Modern materials (graphene, metal foams, titanium, coated metals, LCDs, nanomaterials) have enhanced fixed properties developed through new processes.
  • Smart materials (shape memory alloys, thermochromic pigments, photochromic pigments) change reversibly in response to external stimuli like heat or light.
  • Composites (GRP, CRP) combine materials for improved properties; technical textiles (Kevlar, conductive fabrics, microfibres) are engineered for performance.

lessons.title: Systems Approach to Designing
lessons.description: Electronic systems: inputs, processes and outputs using sensors and microcontrollers.
lessons.content_html:
Systems Approach to Designing

Many products use electronic systems to provide functionality. A security light that switches on when someone approaches, a washing machine that controls water temperature, or a music speaker that amplifies sound — all use a systems approach. Understanding how electronic systems work helps you design products that respond to their environment.

The Input–Process–Output Model

Every electronic system follows the same basic structure: input → process → output. The input component detects a change in the environment (light, temperature, pressure). The process component makes a decision about what to do with that information. The output component performs an action (sound, light, movement).

Key Fact

All electronic systems follow the input → process → output model. Inputs detect changes in the environment; the process makes decisions; outputs perform actions.

Input Devices

Input devices (also called sensors) detect changes and convert them into electrical signals that the system can process.

Light sensors (LDRs) detect light levels. Their resistance changes depending on brightness. Used in automatic streetlights that switch on when it gets dark.

Temperature sensors (thermistors) detect temperature changes. Their resistance decreases as temperature rises. Used in central heating thermostats and car engine monitors.

Pressure sensors detect physical force. Used in car seat sensors (to trigger seatbelt warnings) and digital scales.

Switches are the simplest input devices. They include push switches (doorbells), toggle switches (light switches), tilt switches (detecting orientation) and reed switches (activated by magnets, used in security alarms).

Process: Microcontrollers

The process stage is handled by a microcontroller — a small, programmable computer on a single chip. Microcontrollers can be programmed to act as:

Counters — counting the number of times an event occurs (e.g. counting items on a production line). Timers — triggering actions after a set time (e.g. turning off a light after 30 seconds). Decision makers — using logic to choose between actions based on sensor data (e.g. if temperature is above 25°C, switch on the fan).

Key Fact

Microcontrollers can be programmed as counters (counting events), timers (triggering actions after a set time) and decision makers (choosing actions based on sensor data). They are the “brain” of an electronic system.

Output Devices

Output devices perform the action that the system is designed to produce.

Buzzers produce a simple tone and are used in alarms, timers and doorbells. Speakers produce a wider range of sounds and are used in phones, radios and music systems. Lamps/LEDs produce light and are used for indicators, displays and illumination. Motors produce rotary movement and are used in fans, conveyor belts and electric vehicles.

When designing an electronic system, you need to match the right input, process and output components. For example, a security light system uses a motion sensor (input) connected to a microcontroller (process) that switches on a lamp (output) when movement is detected, then uses a timer to switch it off after a set period.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on systems often give you a scenario and ask you to identify the input, process and output. Always name the specific component (e.g. “thermistor” not just “sensor”) and explain what it does in that context. If the question asks about a microcontroller, state whether it is acting as a counter, timer or decision maker.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All electronic systems follow the input → process → output model, where sensors detect changes, microcontrollers make decisions, and outputs perform actions.
  • Key input devices include light sensors (LDRs), temperature sensors (thermistors), pressure sensors and switches; microcontrollers can act as counters, timers and decision makers.
  • Output devices include buzzers, speakers, lamps/LEDs and motors — the choice depends on the product’s function and the action required.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'systems approach' to designing.
practice_questions.marks: An approach that considers a product as a system of connected components following an input-process-output model (1).

practice_questions.text: Name two types of input sensor and state what each detects.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: light sensor/LDR detects light level (1), temperature sensor/thermistor detects temperature (1), pressure sensor detects force/weight (1), switch detects user action/position (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a microcontroller could be used as a timer in a hand dryer.
practice_questions.marks: The microcontroller is programmed to switch on the heater/fan motor when the pressure sensor is activated (1) and then switch it off automatically after a set time period, e.g. 30 seconds (1).

practice_questions.text: A garden watering system uses a moisture sensor, microcontroller and solenoid valve. Explain how this system works using the input-process-output model.
practice_questions.marks: Input: moisture sensor detects that soil moisture is below a set level (1). Process: microcontroller compares the reading to a threshold and decides to open the valve (1). Output: solenoid valve opens to allow water to flow to the plants (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two output devices and state a product each could be used in.

lessons.title: Mechanical Devices
lessons.description: Types of movement, levers, linkages, cams, gears and pulleys explained.
lessons.content_html:
Mechanical Devices

Mechanical devices are used in products to create movement, change the direction of force or multiply force. Understanding how these mechanisms work is essential for designing products that move. This lesson covers the four types of movement, levers, linkages and rotary systems.

Types of Movement

There are four types of movement (motion) that mechanical devices produce:

Linear motion — movement in a straight line in one direction (e.g. a drawer sliding open). Rotary motion — movement in a circle around a central point (e.g. a wheel turning). Reciprocating motion — backwards-and-forwards movement in a straight line (e.g. a sewing machine needle). Oscillating motion — swinging movement back and forth along an arc (e.g. a pendulum in a clock).

Key Fact

The four types of motion are linear (straight line), rotary (circular), reciprocating (back-and-forth in a line) and oscillating (swinging arc). Many mechanisms convert one type of motion into another.

Levers

A lever is a rigid bar that rotates around a fixed point called the fulcrum. Levers multiply force (making it easier to lift heavy objects) or increase the distance or speed of movement. There are three classes:

First-order lever — the fulcrum is between the effort and the load. Examples: seesaw, crowbar, scissors. These can multiply force or distance depending on where the fulcrum is placed.

Second-order lever — the load is between the fulcrum and the effort. Examples: wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener. These always multiply force (the effort moves further than the load).

Third-order lever — the effort is between the fulcrum and the load. Examples: tweezers, fishing rod, human forearm. These always multiply distance/speed (the load moves further than the effort), but require more force.

Linkages

Linkages are systems of bars connected by pivot points that transmit and change the direction of movement.

A bell crank changes the direction of movement by 90 degrees. When you pull a bicycle brake lever (input), the bell crank converts the pulling motion into a pushing motion that presses the brake pad against the wheel rim. A push/pull linkage (also called a reverse-motion linkage) reverses the direction of input motion — push in one end and the other end pulls out.

Rotary Systems

Rotary systems transmit rotary motion and can change speed, direction or type of movement.

Cams and followers convert rotary motion into reciprocating motion. The cam is a shaped disc on a rotating shaft. As it turns, a follower rides along its edge, moving up and down. The shape of the cam determines the pattern of movement. Used in engines (opening valves) and toys.

Simple gear trains use toothed wheels that mesh together. When gears of different sizes are used, the smaller gear (pinion) turns faster than the larger gear, but with less force (torque). The gear ratio determines the speed and torque relationship. Meshing gears also reverse the direction of rotation.

Pulleys and belts transmit rotary motion between shafts using a belt wrapped around wheels. Like gears, different-sized pulleys change speed and torque. Unlike gears, pulleys connected by a flat belt rotate in the same direction. A crossed belt reverses the direction.

Key Fact

Cams convert rotary to reciprocating motion. Gears transmit rotary motion and can change speed, torque and direction. Pulleys transmit rotary motion over distance using belts. All three are common in exam questions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Mechanical device questions often ask you to identify the type of motion or explain how a mechanism works. Use the correct technical vocabulary — “reciprocating” not “up and down”, “fulcrum” not “pivot point”. If a question involves gears, mention the gear ratio and explain how changing gear size affects speed and torque.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four types of motion are linear, rotary, reciprocating and oscillating — many mechanisms convert between these.
  • Levers (first, second and third order) multiply force or distance; linkages (bell crank, push/pull) change the direction of movement.
  • Rotary systems include cams and followers (rotary to reciprocating), gear trains (change speed, torque and direction) and pulleys and belts (transmit motion over distance).

practice_questions.marks: Oscillating motion (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a bell crank linkage is used in a bicycle brake system.
practice_questions.marks: The bell crank changes the direction of movement by 90 degrees (1). Pulling the brake lever (linear input) is converted by the bell crank into a pushing force that presses the brake pad against the wheel rim (1).

practice_questions.text: A small gear with 20 teeth drives a large gear with 60 teeth. What is the gear ratio and what effect does this have on speed and torque?
practice_questions.marks: Gear ratio is 60:20 = 3:1 (1). The driven gear rotates three times slower than the driver gear (1). The driven gear has three times the torque/turning force (1).

lessons.title: Materials & Their Working Properties
lessons.description: Material categories, types and physical and working properties for all material groups.
lessons.content_html:
Materials & Their Working Properties

Choosing the right material is one of the most important decisions a designer makes. This lesson covers the five main material categories — papers and boards, timbers, metals, polymers and textiles — along with the physical and working properties you need to know for your exam.

Papers & Boards

Papers are thin, flexible sheet materials made from wood pulp. Boards are thicker and more rigid. Key types include:

Papers: bleed-proof paper (for marker pens), cartridge paper (general drawing), grid paper (technical drawing), layout paper (lightweight tracing for design development) and tracing paper (transparent, for copying designs).

Boards: corrugated card (packaging — strong, lightweight, cushioning), duplex board (food packaging), foil-lined board (insulating food containers), foam core board (mounting and model-making), ink jet card (printing) and solid white board (premium packaging).

Natural & Manufactured Timbers

Hardwoods come from broad-leaved, deciduous trees and are generally harder, denser and more expensive. Examples: ash (tough, flexible — tool handles), beech (hard-wearing — furniture), mahogany (attractive grain — furniture), oak (very durable — flooring, outdoor furniture) and balsa (extremely lightweight — model-making).

Softwoods come from coniferous, evergreen trees and grow faster, making them cheaper. Examples: larch (durable outdoors — fencing), pine (versatile — construction, furniture) and spruce (lightweight — construction, musical instruments).

Manufactured boards are made from processed wood. MDF (medium density fibreboard — smooth, easy to shape, good for painting), plywood (layers of veneer glued at right angles — strong in all directions) and chipboard (compressed wood chips — cheap, used in flat-pack furniture).

Key Fact

Hardwoods (oak, mahogany, beech, ash, balsa) are from deciduous trees — harder, denser, more expensive. Softwoods (pine, larch, spruce) are from coniferous trees — faster growing, cheaper. Manufactured boards (MDF, plywood, chipboard) offer consistency in large sheets.

Metals & Alloys

Ferrous metals contain iron. Low carbon steel (mild steel) is cheap and easy to work — used for car bodies, nuts and bolts. Cast iron is very hard but brittle — used for manhole covers and engine blocks. High carbon (tool) steel is extremely hard — used for cutting tools and drill bits.

Non-ferrous metals do not contain iron. Aluminium is lightweight and corrosion-resistant — used for drinks cans and aircraft. Copper is an excellent electrical conductor — used for wiring and plumbing. Tin resists corrosion — used for coating steel cans. Zinc is used for galvanising steel to prevent rust.

Alloys are mixtures of metals. Brass (copper + zinc) is corrosion-resistant and attractive — used for taps and musical instruments. Stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel) resists corrosion — used for cutlery and surgical instruments. High speed steel (HSS) stays hard at high temperatures — used for drill bits.

Thermoforming polymers (thermoplastics) soften when heated and can be reshaped repeatedly. Key examples: acrylic/PMMA (transparent — display cases, signs), HIPS (easy to vacuum form — packaging, yoghurt pots), HDPE (tough — bottles, pipes), polypropylene/PP (flexible hinge — food containers, folders), PVC (durable — window frames, pipes) and PET (clear, strong — drinks bottles).

Thermosetting polymers set permanently when heated and cannot be reshaped. Key examples: epoxy resin/ER (strong adhesive — bonding composites), melamine formaldehyde/MF (heat-resistant — kitchen worktops), phenol formaldehyde/PF (electrical insulator — plugs, handles), polyester resin/PR (used as matrix in GRP/fibreglass) and urea formaldehyde/UF (hard — electrical fittings, adhesive).

Textiles

Natural fibres: cotton (soft, absorbent, breathable — t-shirts, towels), wool (warm, elastic — jumpers, blankets) and silk (smooth, lustrous — scarves, formal wear). Synthetic fibres: polyester (strong, crease-resistant — sportswear), polyamide/nylon (strong, elastic — tights, ropes) and elastane/lycra (very stretchy — sportswear, underwear).

Blended/mixed fibres (e.g. cotton/polyester) combine the best properties of both. Woven fabrics (plain weave — interlocking warp and weft threads) are strong and stable. Non-woven fabrics include bonded fabrics (fibres stuck together — disposable cloths) and felted fabrics (fibres matted by heat/moisture — hats, craft). Knitted fabrics are stretchy and comfortable — used for jumpers, socks and t-shirts.

Key Fact

Textiles include natural (cotton, wool, silk), synthetic (polyester, nylon, elastane) and blended/mixed fibres (cotton/polyester). Fabrics are made by weaving, knitting, bonding or felting.

Physical & Working Properties

You need to know two types of material properties:

Physical properties describe a material's characteristics in its natural state. Absorbency — resistance to moisture (cotton absorbs, polyester resists). Density — mass per unit volume (lead is dense, balsa is not). Fusibility — ability to melt and be reshaped (crucial for casting metals and moulding polymers). Electrical and thermal conductivity — how well a material conducts electricity or heat (copper conducts well, wood does not).

Working properties describe how a material behaves when force is applied. Strength — resistance to breaking under force. Hardness — resistance to scratching or denting. Toughness — ability to absorb impact without fracturing. Malleability — ability to be hammered or pressed into shape. Ductility — ability to be drawn into wire. Elasticity — ability to stretch and return to shape.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Material questions in Section A are often “name” or “state” questions worth 1–2 marks. Learn the key examples for each category. For longer questions, link the material’s properties to why it is suitable for a given product — don’t just name the material, explain the property that makes it the right choice.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five material categories are papers/boards, timbers (hardwoods, softwoods, manufactured boards), metals (ferrous, non-ferrous, alloys), polymers (thermoforming, thermosetting) and textiles (natural, synthetic, blended).
  • Physical properties include absorbency, density, fusibility and conductivity; working properties include strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, ductility and elasticity.
  • Always link a material’s specific properties to the product context — this is how marks are awarded in the exam.

practice_questions.text: Name one hardwood and one softwood. Give a typical use for each.
practice_questions.marks: Any correct hardwood (e.g. oak — flooring/furniture) (1). Any correct softwood (e.g. pine — construction/furniture) (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a ferrous metal and a non-ferrous metal. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Ferrous metals contain iron (1), e.g. low carbon steel/cast iron (1). Non-ferrous metals do not contain iron (1), e.g. aluminium/copper (1). Max 3.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a thermoforming polymer and a thermosetting polymer.
practice_questions.marks: Thermoforming: softens when heated and can be reshaped repeatedly/recyclable (1). Thermosetting: sets permanently when first heated and cannot be reshaped/not recyclable (1).

practice_questions.text: A designer needs a material for a children’s outdoor climbing frame. Explain why they might choose stainless steel.
practice_questions.marks: Stainless steel is very strong/can support children’s weight safely (1). It resists corrosion so won’t rust outdoors in rain (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'malleability' and name a material that is malleable.
practice_questions.marks: The ability to be hammered or pressed into shape without cracking (1). E.g. copper, gold, aluminium (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why cotton/polyester blended fabric might be chosen for a school uniform shirt.
practice_questions.marks: Cotton provides comfort/breathability/absorbency (1). Polyester adds strength/crease resistance/durability so the shirt keeps its shape through regular washing (1).
